chapter.name: Quadrilaterals
chapter.blurb: Definitions and properties of rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums, established by congruence and parallel-line reasoning, plus the angle sum property of any quadrilateral.

scope_in.item: Define a rectangle as a quadrilateral with all four angles 90 degrees, and its equivalent definition as a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other
Prove, using congruent triangles, that a rectangle's diagonals are equal in length, bisect each other, and that a quadrilateral with all four right angles must have equal opposite sides

Define a square as a quadrilateral with all angles 90 degrees and all sides equal, recognise every square as a rectangle, and state its extra diagonal properties (equal, bisecting at 90 degrees, and bisecting the angles)
State and apply the angle sum property that the four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, derived by splitting the quadrilateral with a diagonal into two triangles

Define a parallelogram as a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel, recognise a rectangle as a special parallelogram, and construct a parallelogram from two adjacent sides and the included angle

Prove, using the co-interior and alternate angle properties of parallel lines and congruent triangles, that in a parallelogram opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary, opposite sides are equal, and the diagonals bisect each other without being equal in general
Define a rhombus as a quadrilateral with all four sides equal, recognise every rhombus as a parallelogram, and construct one by fixing two equal adjacent sides and an angle
Use the geoboard activity of perpendicular, equal, bisecting diagonals, and of extending one diagonal, to relate diagonal conditions to a square and to a rhombus that is not a square
Prove that the opposite angles of a rhombus are equal and that its diagonals bisect each other at 90 degrees, and list its full set of properties
Use the activity of joining two congruent triangles (equilateral, isosceles or scalene) along an equal pair of sides to identify the resulting quadrilateral and justify the identification
Define a kite as a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = BC and CD = DA, and state that one diagonal bisects both of its associated angles and is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal

Define a trapezium as a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides, apply the co-interior angle property between its parallel sides, and define an isosceles trapezium as one whose non-parallel sides are equal, with equal angles at each end of a parallel side

Judge, with justification, whether a stated condition on a quadrilateral's angles or diagonals is enough to guarantee it is a particular type (rectangle, square, parallelogram, rhombus or isosceles trapezium)

scope_out.item: Perimeter and area formulas for rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites or trapeziums
scope_out.reason: This chapter studies only angle and diagonal properties derived by congruence; no area or perimeter formula is introduced for any quadrilateral

scope_out.item: Cyclic quadrilaterals and any property connecting quadrilaterals to circles
scope_out.reason: A circle appears only once, as a construction tool in Figure it Out Q3 on p. 94, and no cyclic-quadrilateral property is taught

scope_out.item: Coordinate geometry methods (plotting vertices, using the distance or midpoint formula) to prove a quadrilateral is of a given type
scope_out.reason: Every deduction in the chapter uses congruent triangles and parallel-line transversal properties on an unplaced figure; coordinates are never used

scope_out.item: The angle sum or exterior angle properties of polygons with more than four sides
scope_out.reason: The angle sum result on p. 95 is proved and used only for four-sided figures; it is not generalised to pentagons, hexagons or general polygons

scope_out.item: Line or rotational symmetry of rectangles, squares, rhombuses or kites
scope_out.reason: The chapter's reasoning is entirely about angles, sides and diagonals; symmetry is not mentioned

scope_out.item: Formal two-column geometric proof of a converse (e.g. proving as a numbered Deduction that diagonals bisecting each other implies a parallelogram) -- the book only asks the student to judge true/false and justify briefly (Figure-it-Out, pp. 108-109, already in scope_in), never to write a formal proof of the converse direction
scope_out.reason: The book itself never proves a converse formally; it only poses true/false judgement questions with brief justification

scope_out.item: Tiling, tessellation or symmetry-based paper-folding results beyond identifying the quadrilateral formed
scope_out.reason: The 'Which Quad?' folding game on p. 111 only asks which quadrilateral the creases form; it does not explore tessellation or covering the plane

scope_out.item: Trapeziums that are not isosceles, and any property of their angles beyond the single co-interior angle rule
scope_out.reason: Property 2 (equal angles at the parallel side) is proved only for the isosceles trapezium; a general (scalene) trapezium's non-parallel-side angles have no stated relationship

concepts.name: Rectangles: definition and properties
concepts.description: Two equivalent definitions of a rectangle and its four properties, established by congruence.
concepts.idea: A rectangle can be defined either by its right angles and equal opposite sides, or directly by its equal, bisecting diagonals.
concepts.rule: A rectangle is a quadrilateral in which all four angles are 90 degrees, equivalently a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other. Its opposite sides are equal and parallel, and its diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other.
concepts.example: A door frame with all four corners square (90 degrees) is a rectangle; its two diagonal braces would be equal in length and cross at their midpoints.

questions.q: A carpenter joins two wooden strips of length 12 cm each so that they bisect each other at their midpoints, forming an angle of 70 degrees between them. Will the resulting quadrilateral be a rectangle? Give a reason.
questions.a: Yes. The strips model diagonals of equal length that bisect each other, and this is exactly the condition that makes the quadrilateral formed by their endpoints a rectangle, whatever the angle between them.
s: Identifies that the two strips are equal diagonals that bisect each other
Concludes the shape must be a rectangle regardless of the angle

questions.q: A window frame is made in the shape of a rectangle by joining two diagonal struts of length 40 cm each so that they bisect each other. A workman wants to change the angle between the struts from 90 degrees to 70 degrees, keeping their lengths and the bisecting property the same. Will the frame still be a rectangle? Explain, and state which property would be lost if instead the struts were made unequal in length.
questions.a: Yes, the frame is still a rectangle, because a rectangle only requires the diagonals to be equal and to bisect each other; the angle between them can be anything. If the struts were made unequal in length instead, the diagonals would no longer be equal, so the frame would fail the definition and would not be a rectangle.
s: States the frame remains a rectangle since equal, bisecting diagonals define it, regardless of angle
Explains that the angle between the diagonals is not part of the rectangle condition
Explains that unequal diagonal lengths would break the definition and the shape would not be a rectangle

questions.q: A student claims: 'A quadrilateral with all angles 90 degrees is different from a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other -- they are two different shapes.' Evaluate this claim using the two definitions of a rectangle given in the chapter, and illustrate with the angle values at O when the diagonals of a rectangle meet.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The chapter shows both definitions describe exactly the same class of quadrilaterals: a quadrilateral with all angles 90 degrees always has diagonals that are equal and bisect each other, and equal bisecting diagonals always produce a quadrilateral with all angles 90 degrees. For example, when the diagonals meet at O, the four angles around O can be 70, 110, 70 and 110 degrees for one choice of angle between the struts, or 90, 90, 90 and 90 degrees for another, yet in both cases the quadrilateral formed still has all four corner angles equal to 90 degrees.
s: States the claim is wrong, since both definitions describe the same class of quadrilaterals
Explains the two definitions are shown to be equivalent by the chapter's deductions
Gives an example of angles at O to illustrate that the corner angles stay 90 degrees regardless

questions.a: The reasoning is not enough. Equal opposite sides alone make ABCD a parallelogram, not necessarily a rectangle; the angles must also be shown to be 90 degrees, or, equivalently, the diagonals must be shown to be equal.
s: States the reasoning is insufficient
Explains that equal opposite sides alone only guarantee a parallelogram, and the right-angle or equal-diagonal condition is missing

Explains this works because equal, bisecting diagonals define a rectangle

concepts.name: Squares: definition and properties
concepts.description: A square as a special rectangle with all sides equal, and its extra diagonal properties.
concepts.idea: Because a square is a rectangle with the extra condition of equal sides, it inherits every rectangle property and gains two more about its diagonals.
concepts.rule: A square is a quadrilateral with all angles equal to 90 degrees and all sides of equal length. Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square. In a square, the diagonals are equal, bisect each other at 90 degrees, and bisect the angles of the square.
concepts.example: A square floor tile of side 4 units has diagonals that cross at right angles and each cuts a 90 degree corner into two 45 degree angles.

concepts.name: The angle sum of a quadrilateral
concepts.description: Splitting any quadrilateral into two triangles by a diagonal to show its four angles always add to 360 degrees.
concepts.idea: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles, and each triangle's angles add to 180 degrees, so the whole quadrilateral's angles add to double that.
concepts.rule: The sum of all four angles in any quadrilateral is 360 degrees. This is why a quadrilateral cannot have three right angles unless the fourth is also a right angle.
concepts.example: A quadrilateral with angles 100, 80 and 70 degrees must have a fourth angle of 360 - 100 - 80 - 70 = 110 degrees.

concepts.name: Parallelograms: definition and properties
concepts.description: Quadrilaterals with both pairs of opposite sides parallel, and the angle, side and diagonal properties this gives.
concepts.idea: Treating the parallel sides as transversal pairs shows adjacent angles are supplementary and opposite angles are equal, and matching congruent triangles across a diagonal shows the sides and diagonals behave in a fixed way.
concepts.rule: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral in which both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Its opposite sides are equal, its adjacent angles add up to 180 degrees while its opposite angles are equal, and its diagonals bisect each other, but need not be equal and need not meet at a right angle. Every rectangle is a parallelogram.
concepts.example: A parallelogram with one angle 30 degrees has adjacent angles of 150, 30 and 150 degrees in order round the shape.

concepts.name: Rhombus: definition and properties
concepts.description: A quadrilateral with all sides equal, its angle properties inherited from being a parallelogram, and its extra diagonal properties.
concepts.idea: A rhombus turns out to be a special parallelogram, since equal adjacent sides force its opposite sides to be parallel, so it keeps every parallelogram property and adds two more about its diagonals.
concepts.rule: A rhombus is a quadrilateral in which all four sides have the same length. Every rhombus is a parallelogram, so its adjacent angles add up to 180 degrees and its opposite angles are equal. In addition, the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at an angle of 90 degrees, and they bisect the angles of the rhombus.
concepts.example: A rhombus with one angle 50 degrees has angles 50, 130, 50 and 130 degrees in order, and its diagonals cross at right angles.

concepts.name: Kite and trapezium
concepts.description: A kite as two pairs of adjacent equal sides with a perpendicular bisecting diagonal, and a trapezium as a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides, including the isosceles case.
concepts.idea: Joining two triangles that share a base along their equal sides can produce a kite, while simply relaxing a parallelogram to needing only one pair of parallel sides gives a trapezium.
concepts.rule: A kite is a quadrilateral that can be labelled ABCD so that AB equals BC and CD equals DA; one of its diagonals bisects both of its angles at those vertices and is perpendicular to, and bisects, the other diagonal. A trapezium is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides; when its non-parallel sides are equal it is called an isosceles trapezium, and then the angles at each end of a parallel side are equal.
concepts.example: Joining two isosceles triangles of sides 8, 8 and 6 cm along their unequal 6 cm sides can give a kite; a trapezium PQRS with PQ parallel to SR has angle S + angle P = 180 degrees.

questions.a: The claim is wrong. Two pairs of adjacent equal sides, AB = BC and CD = DA, is exactly the definition of a kite, and a kite need not have all four sides equal. The extra condition needed to make it a rhombus is that the two pairs must also equal each other, that is AB = BC = CD = DA, giving all four sides the same length.

States the extra condition of all four sides being equal, turning it into a rhombus
